newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI criticises high deficits but rejects EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: EMI criticises high deficits but rejects EMU delay.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) on Tuesday voiced angst about persistently high deficit levels in many EU states but said there was still a more than even chance that the euro single currency would be launched as planned in January 1999.

Speaking at a news conference after the publication of the EMI's 1996 annual report, president Alexandre Lamfalussy said he was opposed to any delay in the single currency's launch because the risks of such a move would be too great.
"I am not in favour of a delay because I think the risks are considerable," he said. "It could wreck the whole project."
With EU economies on a "fundamental convergence track" the chance of economic and monetary union (EMU) starting on time was "significantly more than 50 percent," he added.

In its annual report, the forerunner of the European Central Bank said the fiscal situation in many nations remained far from satisfactory, but warned EMU-hopefuls aginst using one-off accounting tricks to bring budget deficits down.
"Fiscal consolidation has continued and there has been a broad but relatively small decline in the overall deficit for the Union," Lamfalussy told the news conference.
"But deficit levels are still too high, and we are not entirely happy with the way the decline has happened."
Raising revenues, rather than cutting government spending, was not the right approach, he said, adding that deficit reduction should be the "outcome of a basic reform process"

The Maastricht Treaty, which sets out the timetable and entry criteria for monetary union, calls for budget deficits to be at most three percent of gross domestic product and debt to be no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Statistics compiled by the EMI, showed that last autumn, the overall EU debt position was 73.5 percent of GDP and its deficit level was 4.4 percent -- well over target.

Lamfalussy stressed, however, that the data forming the basis of the report dated from 1996, saying it was not a forecast. "(The report) does not contain implicit or explicit guesses on the likely outcome of next year, or even this year."

On inflation and interest rates, the EMI was more upbeat, saying that inflationary pressure had been brought under control in a large number of countries and that a number of nations had effectively already achieved price stability.

But Lamfalussy said he would welcome more effort in the coming months to convince financial markets and the general public that monetary policy directed at sustained growth and low inflation was not being followed for EMU alone.

"Market fears have been generally about (convergence) efforts being pursued exclusively for Maastricht purposes," he said. "The stability-oriented monetary policies followed now by all EU central banks are here to stay. It will be in the interests of everyone that governments make this clear. I would very much welcome confirmation of this."

Asked about the eventual interpretation of the Maastricht criteria in determining the "ins and "outs" of the first round of monetary union Lamfalussy was quick to stress that "the letter and the spirit of the Treaty" must be respected.

The Treaty contained three key factors: It set target ratios for budget deficits and public debt, it accepted deviation from those values, and it insisted on sustainability. "One has to use all three elements at the same time," he said.

While reluctant to make specific predictions on who would be in the first round of EMU, Lamfalussy said a start with Germany was "rather improbable" and added that significant EMU progress had been made by all countries -- including the so-called "Club Med" nations of Italy, Spain and Portugal.
Economists said the EMI report had dimmed the chances of a broad euro starting line and would serve as a clear reminder that entry is not a foregone conclusion for all euro hopefuls.
"The EMI has fired a warning shot to tell the markets that a lot of work is still to be done," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank in London.

But they said the stern tone of the report should not be taken purely on its own, since it was becoming clearer by the day that politics, and not economics, would take a dominant role in determining the first EMU entrants.
"If monetary union were left purely down to the EMI, then you could say this report is bad news for the broad EMU story," said Darren Wiliams, European economist at UBS in London.
"But the EMI is only one of the two bodies which will advise on suitable EMU candidates, and we all suspect that the European Commission we have a dominant role in that."

With only about a year to go before the EC makes a final decision, based on 1997 data, as to which states qualify, the EMI urged governments to remain vigilant in curbing inflation and avoid any setbacks in the consolidation of public finances.

"The stance adopted in the period ahead will be particularly important in that it will increasingly affect inflation in 1999 and thereafter and hence price expectations for the euro area," the report said.
